title: Who the agent acts as: per-user credentials and permission layers

What you will be able to do

Shared service identity versus acting on behalf of each user

Every tool call an agent makes runs under some identity. Often that identity is a single service credential that all users share. Two gaps follow from that choice. Each user gets whatever that credential can reach, not what they personally are allowed to reach. And downstream audit logs show one service account, so nobody can tell which end user caused an action. The safer design is for the agent to act as each user, holding a token issued to that user.

Claude Managed Agents builds this model into vaults. A vault is the collection of credentials for one end user. You register it once and pass its ID when you create a session, so the agent definition stays shared while the credentials change per session. MCP credentials (
) are keyed by
and injected automatically when the agent connects to that server. For

, Anthropic refreshes the access token on your behalf if you supply a refresh block. Credential values are write-only and never returned by the API. In Claude Code, managed MCP configuration supports the same pattern: OAuth or per-user headers let each user authenticate as themselves.
Attaching one end user's vault to a session
python
Three runtime rules decide whose identity a call actually uses, and each one can open a gap if you overlook it:

If no credential matches the server URL, the connection is attempted unauthenticated. It fails only if the server requires authentication, so a server that allows anonymous access will quietly serve anonymous data.
If several vaults hold a matching credential, the first vault with a match wins. Passing a shared vault ahead of a user's vault makes every call run as the shared identity.
In multiagent sessions, vault credentials apply to every thread. Every subagent whose definition declares that server acts as the same user.

Keeping credentials outside the agent's boundary

An agent that reads untrusted content can be prompt-injected. If it holds a secret, an injected instruction can try to send that secret somewhere. The robust fix is to make sure the agent never has the secret. Vault environment-variable credentials work this way. The sandbox holds only an opaque placeholder, which is swapped for the real value at egress, so
the agent never sees the secret value
. Setting
to header-only narrows this further. Request bodies are often built from content the agent is working with, so the body is the larger exposure surface.

Substitution only applies to requests going out. If a client uses the stored secret to fetch a session token, for example through an OAuth client-credentials grant, the returned token arrives in the sandbox unredacted. For exchange-based flows, perform the exchange yourself and store the resulting token in the vault.
Self-hosted Agent SDK deployments get the same property from a proxy outside the agent's container. Run the container with

, which removes every network interface, and mount a Unix socket connected to a proxy on the host. The proxy injects credentials, enforces an endpoint allowlist and logs every request. The agent sees only the tool interface. A prompt-injected request to an attacker's domain then has no network path except through a proxy that refuses it.

Two details decide whether the proxy actually works. First, injecting a credential into HTTPS traffic means the proxy has to read the request, so it must terminate TLS, for example with mitmproxy. The proxy's CA certificate then goes into the agent's trust store. A plain forward proxy only relays the encrypted tunnel and can neither inspect nor inject. Second, setting

on its own is not a boundary, because not every tool reads those variables: plain ssh and most database drivers ignore them. Removing the network interface enforces the boundary whatever the tool does. Give the agent's service account minimal IAM permissions, not broad ones, and route sensitive access through the proxy where possible.
On the exam

For exfiltration questions, choose controls that hold regardless of what the model decides: no direct network interface, credentials injected outside the boundary, and a TLS-terminating proxy that can inspect traffic. Broad IAM on the agent, proxy environment variables on their own, and trusting the model's judgment all fail once the model is persuaded.
Exam trap
Setting HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY is enough to force all agent traffic through a credential-injecting proxy.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 3 of 7
Check yourself

Your agent reads untrusted web content. It holds a client secret as a vault environment_variable credential, and inside the sandbox it runs an OAuth client-credentials grant to get an API access token. A reviewer flags this as a gap. Why, and what is the fix?
The access token returned by the exchange reaches the sandbox unredacted, so do the exchange outside the agent and store the resulting token in the vault
The client secret travels in the request body, so set injection_location to header-only and the returned token will also stay hidden
There is no gap: vault substitution keeps every credential derived from the secret out of the sandbox, so the access token is redacted as well
The placeholder cannot be exchanged for a token, so put the real client secret directly in the sandbox environment instead
Checkpoint 4 of 7
Exam question

A security architect is designing an Agent SDK deployment that will process untrusted third-party documents and must prevent credential exfiltration even if a prompt injection convinces the agent to try to send data to an attacker-controlled endpoint. Which combination of controls together address this threat, given that TLS-encrypted traffic through a plain forward proxy cannot be inspected or have credentials injected into it? (Select 3)
(Select
Run the agent in a container with --network none and route all outbound calls through a Unix socket to a proxy on the host, so the agent has no direct network interface at all
Keep credentials outside the agent's security boundary entirely, injecting them at a proxy so the agent only ever sends requests without the underlying secret
Deploy a TLS-terminating proxy with its CA certificate trusted in the agent's environment so encrypted HTTPS traffic can be inspected and have credentials injected before re-encryption

Set HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY environment variables alone, since every tool the agent might invoke respects these variables and a standard forward proxy can inject credentials into an encrypted tunnel
Grant the agent process broad IAM permissions directly so it can reach any downstream service on its own, without depending on any proxy being available or reachable
Rely on the model's built-in judgment to avoid contacting suspicious domains instead of enforcing any network-level boundary that would hold regardless of the model's own decisions

Which permission layer actually decides a tool call

Credentials control what the agent can reach. The Agent SDK's permission flow controls which calls it actually makes. The flow is a fixed sequence, and the first step that resolves a call ends the evaluation. A security control placed late in the sequence only sees calls that no earlier step settled.
Agent SDK permission evaluation order: the first step that resolves the call wins
Step
What it does
Under bypassPermissions
1. Hooks
Run custom code to allow, deny or modify the request
Still run; a deny is enforced
2. Deny rules
Block matching calls (disallowed_tools)
Still enforced
3. Ask rules
Send matching calls for approval
Still route the call to canUseTool
4. Permission mode
Mode-based approvals
Approves everything reaching it except rm/rmdir of a critical path
5. Allow rules
Auto-approve listed tools (allowed_tools)
Rarely reached
6. canUseTool callback
Runtime approval when no earlier step resolved the call
Reached only by calls that fall through
Predict first
An agent is configured with allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"] in default mode. Claude tries to call Write. What happens?
Write is denied outright, because it is not on the list
Write is unavailable, because only listed tools can run
The call falls through to the permission mode and then the canUseTool callback
The sequence explains a common audit finding. A team sets

callback that logs requests and denies anything touching a credentials directory. The callback almost never runs. It is invoked only when the flow falls through to a prompt, and calls auto-approved by

Tool reach is an authorization question too. An agent that can load any MCP server can call tools no one has reviewed, so the gap is closed by deciding which servers and tools exist at all, through
controlling MCP servers, plugins and hooks through policy
. At the SDK and settings level, one deny rule removes every MCP tool, across all servers, until specific ones are approved.

Exam question

While auditing an Agent SDK integration, you find allowed_tools=["Read", "Glob", "Grep", "Bash"] combined with permission_mode="bypassPermissions", and a canUseTool callback that logs every request and denies anything touching a credentials directory. The developer believed this callback was their safety net. What should the audit conclude?
The callback is shadowed: calls approved earlier in the order, including everything bypassPermissions approves, never reach canUseTool; a PreToolUse hook is needed if every call must be checked
The callback is functioning as intended, because bypassPermissions only affects tools not already listed in allowed_tools, and Bash was never explicitly allowed so it still reaches the callback
The callback is functioning as intended, because canUseTool is always invoked first in the order, before permission mode or allow rules are ever considered
The callback is shadowed only for MCP tools with the requiresUserInteraction metadata flag, while ordinary built-in tools like Bash still reach the callback as expected

Exam question

A CISO reviewing an Agent SDK rollout learns that permission_mode is set to bypassPermissions in a batch-processing pipeline and asks which authorization controls, if any, still constrain the agent under that mode. Based on how bypassPermissions is evaluated, which of the following statements are accurate? (Select 2)
(Select
Hooks still execute and a hook that denies a call is still enforced, because hooks are evaluated before the permission mode step in the flow
An explicit ask rule configured in settings.json still forces the call through the canUseTool callback, even though the mode would otherwise auto-approve it
allowed_tools still meaningfully restricts which tools are auto-approved, so listing only a narrow set of tools there keeps bypassPermissions scoped to just those tools
disallowed_tools entries for whole tool names have no effect once bypassPermissions is active, since the mode is designed to override every other layer of the permission system
The plan permission mode and bypassPermissions produce identical behavior for file-edit tools, since both ultimately approve or deny edits at the same evaluation step
